course.title: How memory sticks
course.subtitle: The science behind spaced repetition and self-testing
course.description: Two short modules on why we forget and which study habits actually make learning last.
course.author: Interactive Learning Studio sample

modules.title: Why we forget
modules.summary: The forgetting curve, and why spreading practice out beats cramming.
objectives: Describe the shape of the forgetting curve
Tell massed practice apart from distributed practice

lesson.text: In 1885 Hermann Ebbinghaus published the first careful experiments on memory. He memorised lists of nonsense syllables, such as *DAX* or *BOK*, and measured how much he retained over time.
Retention drops **fast at first** and then levels off. Most of what is lost goes in the first day or two; what survives that period fades much more slowly.

lesson.title: Savings
lesson.text: Even when Ebbinghaus could no longer recall a list, relearning it took fewer repetitions than learning it the first time. That reduction is called **savings**, and it shows that a faded memory is not completely gone.
The same amount of study time produces longer-lasting memories when it is split into sessions spread over days than when it is packed into one sitting.
Review just as something starts to slip. Each successful review lets you wait a little longer before the next one — that is exactly what the flashcard schedule in this site does.

keyTerms.definition: The pattern in which memory drops steeply soon after learning and then declines more slowly.
Study spread across separate sessions produces better long-term retention than the same time in one session.
Studying material in one long, uninterrupted block; cramming.
The reduced effort needed to relearn something compared with learning it the first time.

modules.title: Retrieval practice
modules.summary: Why testing yourself teaches more than re-reading, and how to make practice usefully hard.
objectives: Spot the illusion of competence in your own study

lesson.text: Pulling information out of memory changes the memory itself. Each successful retrieval makes the next one easier — an effect known as the **testing effect** or **retrieval practice**.
In a well-known 2006 study, students who read a passage once and then took recall tests remembered more a week later than students who re-read it several times.

Interestingly, the re-reading group did better on a test given just five minutes later. Re-reading feels effective because the material becomes ==familiar==, but familiarity is not the same as being able to recall it.
Robert Bjork described conditions that slow learning down in the moment but improve long-term retention. Three of the best supported are:

items: **Interleaving** — mixing different kinds of problems instead of practising one kind in a block

lesson.title: The illusion of competence
lesson.text: Highlighting and re-reading make material feel known. Test yourself before deciding you have learned something.

lesson.title: Try it
lesson.text: Close this lesson and write down the three desirable difficulties from memory. Then check.

keyTerms.definition: Retrieving information from memory strengthens it more than restudying the same information.
A learning condition that feels harder now but leads to better long-term retention.
Mixing different topics or problem types within one practice session.
Mistaking familiarity with material for the ability to recall or use it.

items.prompt: According to the forgetting curve, when is most information lost?
options: In the first day or two after learning
Steadily at the same rate for weeks
Only after about a month
Only if the material was never understood
items.explanation: Retention falls steeply right after learning and then levels off. A steady, constant loss would be a straight line, not a curve.

items.prompt: Two students each study for three hours. Ana studies the night before the exam; Ben studies one hour on each of three days. What does the spacing effect predict a month later?
options: Ben remembers more
Ana remembers more
Both remember the same, since total time is equal
Neither remembers anything
items.explanation: Total time is the same, but distributing it across sessions gives more durable memories. Equal time does not mean equal retention.

options: Relearning a forgotten list took fewer repetitions than learning it first
Memories that cannot be recalled are permanently erased
Nonsense syllables are easier to learn than real words
Sleep has no effect on memory
items.explanation: Savings means some trace remains even when recall fails, so relearning is faster.

items.prompt: Which of these are examples of distributed practice?
options: Reviewing vocabulary for 10 minutes every morning
Reading a whole textbook chapter five times in one evening
Revisiting last week's notes before starting new material
Doing all practice problems the night before the test
items.explanation: Distributed practice spreads sessions over time. The other two pack everything into one sitting.

items.prompt: Cramming usually feels less productive than spacing while you are doing it.
items.explanation: Cramming tends to feel fluent and productive, which is part of why people rely on it. Spacing feels harder.

items.prompt: Ebbinghaus used nonsense syllables so that prior knowledge would not affect the results.
items.explanation: Meaningless syllables gave him material with no existing associations to lean on.

items.front: When did Ebbinghaus publish his memory experiments?

items.prompt: Explain to a friend why studying in several short sessions beats one long session, even when the total time is the same.
items.answer: Memories fade quickly after learning. When you come back after a gap and recall the material again, the memory is strengthened and fades more slowly afterwards. One long session gives no chance for that cycle, so the material feels well known at the end but is forgotten fast.
keyPoints: Memory fades quickly after learning (forgetting curve)
Coming back after a gap strengthens the memory
Cramming feels effective but fades quickly

items.prompt: Match each idea to what it means.

pairs.right: Steep early loss, then a slow decline
Spread-out sessions beat one long session
Relearning is faster than first learning

items.explanation: These four ideas come from the earliest research on memory and still underpin study advice today.

items.prompt: In the 2006 retrieval-practice study, which group did better on a test one week later?
options: Students who read once and then practised recalling
Students who re-read the passage several times
Both groups scored the same
Students who highlighted while reading
items.explanation: The re-reading group did better after five minutes, but the recall group remembered more a week later.

items.prompt: A student rereads her notes until they feel familiar and concludes she is ready. What is the main risk?
options: She is mistaking familiarity for the ability to recall
She has spaced her study too widely
She has interleaved too many topics
She has tested herself too often
items.explanation: This is the illusion of competence: recognising material is easier than producing it from memory.

options: Mixing area, volume and ratio problems in one set
Twenty area problems, then twenty volume problems
Re-reading the chapter on area twice
Watching a video on volume
items.explanation: Interleaving mixes problem types so you must choose the right method each time, instead of repeating one method in a block.

items.prompt: Which of these are desirable difficulties?
options: Spacing reviews over several days
Testing yourself instead of re-reading
Highlighting key sentences
Mixing problem types in one session
items.explanation: Highlighting feels productive but does not make retrieval harder or more effortful, so it is not a desirable difficulty.

items.prompt: If practice feels easy and smooth, you are probably learning efficiently.
items.explanation: Smooth, easy practice often signals familiarity, not durable learning. Some difficulty is a good sign.

items.prompt: Retrieving something from memory changes how well you will remember it later.
items.explanation: That is the testing effect: retrieval strengthens the memory being retrieved.

items.prompt: Design a one-week study plan for a chapter using what you learned. Describe what you would do and why.
items.answer: Read the chapter once, then close it and write down what I remember. Over the next days, test myself with questions rather than re-reading, with gaps of a day or two between sessions. Mix questions from this chapter with earlier ones. Check answers after each attempt and spend more time on what I got wrong.
keyPoints: Checking answers and focusing on mistakes

items.prompt: Match each study habit to the principle it uses (or breaks).
